content: The evidence regarding the impact of mass drug administration (MDA) on all-cause hospitalizations within the first month after MDA is uncertain. Similarly, the effect of MDA on hospitalizations due to severe malaria during the same period is unclear, based on data from a single observational study. Changes in hospital admissions for severe malaria ranged from a 31% decrease to an 8% increase after the first round of MDA, and from a 19% decrease to an 8% increase after the second round. Statistically significant changes were observed at three of eight time points. However, due to the lack of data on sample sizes and non-MDA control areas, absolute effects could not be calculated. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. The effect of MDA on parasitologically confirmed malaria cases within the first month post-MDA is also uncertain. Observational data suggest reductions in confirmed cases ranging from 35% to 62% after the first round of MDA and 26% to 58% after the second round. These reductions were statistically significant, but similar decreases were observed in non-MDA control areas, and confidence intervals overlapped at most time points. The lack of data on sample sizes further limits the ability to calculate absolute effects. A systematic review of eight cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) conducted in six countries with low malaria transmission (Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Tanzania, Vietnam, and Zambia) assessed the impact of MDA on Plasmodium falciparum prevalence and incidence. Most studies conducted three rounds of MDA within one year, while others conducted one to four rounds over varying timeframes. Meta-analyses showed reductions in P. falciparum prevalence and incidence 1–3 months after the last MDA round, but no impact on clinical disease. Longer-term outcomes showed no effect or were of very low certainty. In moderateto high-transmission settings, two cRCTs and two non-randomized studies (NRSs) from four countries (Burkina Faso, Gambia, Nigeria, and Zambia) evaluated MDA. The cRCTs showed little to no effect on P. falciparum prevalence or clinical malaria incidence, with low to moderate certainty. NRSs suggested a slight reduction in prevalence at 4–12 and 12–24 months, but evidence was of low certainty. For Plasmodium vivax, five cRCTs and seven NRSs from eight countries (Cambodia, India, Kenya, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Panama, Solomon Islands, Venezuela, and Vietnam) assessed MDA. All cRCTs used dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP), with some also administering low-dose primaquine. However, none used sufficient 8-aminoquinoline dosages to achieve radical cure of P. vivax hypnozoites. Meta-analyses showed MDA may reduce P. vivax prevalence 1–3 months after the last round, but no impact was observed at later time points. Evidence from NRSs was of very low certainty. One cRCT without 8-aminoquinoline found no increase in severe adverse events within 0–3 months post-MDA. Overall, the evidence on MDA's impact on malaria transmission, clinical outcomes, and adverse events is limited by serious risks of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency. While MDA may reduce malaria prevalence in some settings, its long-term effects and safety remain uncertain.
